nationality_or_literary_tradition: Saint Lucian; poet and playwright writing in English and Saint Lucian Creole, resident for long periods in Trinidad and the United States
literary_identity: Saint Lucian poet and playwright, Nobel laureate, who made the Caribbean archipelago the matter of an epic poetry in English and Creole, from In a Green Night to Omeros
biography: Derek Alton Walcott was born on 23 January 1930 in Castries, Saint Lucia, the son of Warwick Walcott, a civil servant and sometime watercolourist who died when Derek was a year old, and Alix Maarlin, a teacher who ran a school in their house and recited poetry to her children. A twin, he was educated at Saint Mary's College in Castries and at the University College of the West Indies in Jamaica, taking a degree in 1953. He published his first poems in a private pamphlet at eighteen, founded the Saint Lucia Arts Guild in 1950, and made his name with the play Henri Christophe (1950) and the collection In a Green Night: Poems 1948-1960 (1962). He lived and taught in Trinidad from 1959 to 1976, founded the Trinidad Theatre Workshop in 1959 and wrote the plays of Dream on Monkey Mountain and Other Plays (1970); his poetry went on through The Castaway (1965), The Gulf (1969), Another Life (1973), Sea Grapes (1976), The Star-Apple Kingdom (1979), The Fortunate Traveller (1981) and Midsummer (1984) to the epic Omeros (1990), which many critics regard as his masterpiece. He was professor of poetry and creative writing at Boston University from 1981 to 2007. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992, the T. S. Eliot Prize in 2011 for White Egrets, and died at Cap Estate, Saint Lucia, on 17 March 2017.
literary_profile: Poetry: 25 Poems (1948), Epitaph for the Young (1949), Poems (1951), In a Green Night (1962), Selected Poems (1964), The Castaway (1965), The Gulf (1969), Another Life (1973), Sea Grapes (1976), The Star-Apple Kingdom (1979), The Fortunate Traveller (1981), Midsummer (1984), The Arkansas Testament (1987), Omeros (1990), The Bounty (1997), Tiepolo's Hound (2000), The Prodigal (2004), Selected Poems (2007) and White Egrets (2010). Plays: Henri Christophe (1950), The Sea at Dauphin (1954), Dream on Monkey Mountain (1970), The Joker of Seville and O Babylon! (1978) and Remembrance and Pantomime (1980). Essays: What the Twilight Says (1998).
stylistic_characteristics: Long, meditative, densely metaphorical poems in a syntactically elaborate English, set against the plain vernacular speech of Creole characters (Shabine, Achille); the hexameters and terza rima of Omeros; a habit of reading the Caribbean landscape through Homer, Dante and the Bible without letting the classical frame master it; the poet as painter, making and unmaking his island.
intellectual_concerns: Colonial history and the Middle Passage; the divided self of the Caribbean artist ('I have Dutch, nigger, and English in me, and either I'm nobody, or I'm a nation'); the sea, the fishermen and the landscape of Saint Lucia; exile and return; love, age and mortality (White Egrets); the vocation of poetry itself.
historical_significance: The foremost poet of the anglophone Caribbean, who with Omeros gave the region its epic and in doing so reopened the epic as a living form for postcolonial writing; Nobel laureate in 1992 and the model for two generations of Caribbean poets.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia and the Oxford Research Encyclopedia, with the contents of Selected Poems: the collections from 25 Poems (1948) to White Egrets (2010) and the main plays. Installment 10 records only the four Norton selections, 'A Far Cry from Africa' (collected 1962), 'The Schooner Flight' (1979), 'The Season of Phantasmal Peace' (1981) and Omeros (1990), so the bibliography is incomplete; the plays have no records and the date of first publication of 'A Far Cry from Africa' is given as 1962, the date of the collection.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, translator and children's writer, Poet Laureate 1984-1998
literary_identity: English poet of the animal and the elemental, Poet Laureate from 1984, whose sequences Wodwo and Crow and the late Birthday Letters changed the sound of postwar English verse
biography: Edward James Hughes was born on 17 August 1930 at Mytholmroyd, in the Calder Valley of West Yorkshire, the youngest of the three children of Edith Farrar and William Henry Hughes, a joiner who had survived the First World War and ran a shop in the village. The family moved to Mexborough, in South Yorkshire, when he was seven, and the landscape of millstone grit and moorland of his childhood remained the ground of his poetry. He read English at Pembroke College, Cambridge, where he met Sylvia Plath, whom he married in 1956; they lived in the United States and then in Devon, and she killed herself in 1963. His first collection, The Hawk in the Rain (1957), won the New York Poetry Center's first publication award and made his name; Lupercal (1960) and Wodwo (1967) followed, and Crow (1970), the sequence of poems about a trickster bird, became his most influential book. He wrote the radio play Under Milk Wood's successor in his own idiom, the children's book The Iron Man (1968), and many volumes of translations and of poems for children; Gaudete (1977), Cave Birds (1978), Moortown (1979) and River (1983) came before he was appointed Poet Laureate in 1984. His later books include Flowers and Insects (1986), Wolfwatching (1989), the Ovid translations of Tales from Ovid (1997) and Birthday Letters (1998), the poems to Plath. He died in London on 28 October 1998.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Hawk in the Rain (1957), Lupercal (1960), Wodwo (1967), Crow (1970), Gaudete (1977), Cave Birds (1978), Moortown (1979), River (1983), Flowers and Insects (1986), Wolfwatching (1989), Rain-Charm for the Duchy (1992), New Selected Poems 1957-1994 (1995), Tales from Ovid (1997) and Birthday Letters (1998); Collected Poems, ed. Paul Keegan (2003). Plays and prose: The Iron Man (1968), Seneca's Oedipus (1969), Shakespeare and the Goddess of Complete Being (1992) and Winter Pollen (1994).
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry of hard stresses and dense consonantal sound, built on the cadence of Anglo-Saxon and of Hughes's Yorkshire speech; violent, exact imagery of animals, weather and machinery; repetitive, chant-like sequences in Crow and Cave Birds; the late poems in Birthday Letters plainer, quieter and more colloquial.
intellectual_concerns: The violence and energy of the natural world (hawks, pike, wind, the moor); the brute fact of animal existence as a rebuke to human consciousness; myth, folklore and the occult (Crow, Cave Birds, Gaudete); the First World War and the Yorkshire landscape of his childhood (Moortown, Remains of Elmet); marriage, bereavement and memory (Birthday Letters).
historical_significance: The dominant English poet of his generation and, as Poet Laureate from 1984, the public face of poetry in Britain for fourteen years; Crow and the animal poems changed the register of postwar English verse, and Birthday Letters became one of the best-selling and most discussed volumes of poetry of the century.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia, the Faber Collected Poems contents and general knowledge: the collections from The Hawk in the Rain (1957) to Birthday Letters (1998), with the plays and prose. Installment 10 records only the six Norton selections ('Wind', 1957; 'Pike', 1960; 'Out' and 'Theology', 1967; 'Crow's Last Stand' and 'Crow Tyrannosaurus', 1970), so the bibliography is incomplete; the books have no records and the children's books were not checked.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; novelist, poet, critic and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Nigerian novelist whose Things Fall Apart gave modern African literature its founding book and whose later fiction and essays carried the argument about the African writer, colonialism and the English language
biography: Albert Chinualumogu Achebe was born on 16 November 1930 in Ogidi, in the Igbo country of eastern Nigeria, the son of Isaiah Okafo Achebe, a teacher and evangelist of the Church Missionary Society, and Janet Anaenechi Iloegbunam; he grew up between the mission and the traditional religion of his grandfather's generation. He was educated at the Government College in Umuahia and at the University College, Ibadan, where he read English and became critical of the way Western literature represented Africa. He taught briefly and joined the Nigerian Broadcasting Service in Lagos in 1954; Things Fall Apart appeared in 1958, followed by No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964) and A Man of the People (1966). He was a founder and the first editor of the Heinemann African Writers Series. During the Biafran war (1967-1970) he supported Biafran independence and worked for its cause abroad; the poems of Beware, Soul Brother (1971) and the stories of Girls at War (1972) came out of the war, and his essay collection Morning Yet on Creation Day (1975) includes 'The Novelist as Teacher' and his reply to Conrad, 'An Image of Africa' (1975). A car crash in 1990 left him partly paralysed and he moved to the United States, teaching at Bard College and, from 2009, at Brown University. Anthills of the Savannah (1987) was his last novel. He won the Man Booker International Prize in 2007 and died in Boston on 21 March 2013.
literary_profile: Novels: Things Fall Apart (1958), No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964), A Man of the People (1966) and Anthills of the Savannah (1987). Stories: The Sacrificial Egg (1962), Girls at War and Other Stories (1972) and African Short Stories (1985, edited with C. L. Innes). Poetry: Beware, Soul Brother (1971) and Collected Poems (2004). Essays: Morning Yet on Creation Day (1975), Hopes and Impediments (1988), The Education of a British-Protected Child (2009) and There Was a Country (2012). Children's books: Chike and the River (1966), How the Leopard Got His Claws (1972) and The Flute (1977).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, measured English that carries the rhythm and idiom of Igbo speech, built out of proverbs, folk-tales and the cadences of the King James Bible; an ironic narrative manner that lets a community's own language judge its actions; the mature novels combine a large historical span with a tight, dramatic scene; the stories of the war are short, bare and unsparing.
intellectual_concerns: The collision of Igbo tradition and colonial Christianity (Things Fall Apart); the corruption and disillusionment of independence (No Longer at Ease, A Man of the People); the Biafran war and its aftermath (Girls at War, 'Civil Peace'); the responsibility of the African writer and the politics of language; masculinity, gender and the exercise of power in the Igbo world.
historical_significance: The founding novel of modern African literature in English, translated into more than fifty languages and taught across the world; Achebe is called the father of modern African writing, a title he rejected, and his essays on Conrad and on the African writer set the terms of the postcolonial debate about the English language and the African novel.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia's list and general knowledge: the five novels, the story collections, the poetry and essay collections and the children's books listed. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Civil Peace' (1971), so the bibliography is incomplete; the novels, which would have their own records in a complete bibliography of the author, are not recorded here, and the dates of the essay collections were not checked title by title.
